claim: DNMT1 inhibitor GSK3484862 treatment for 3 days led to minimal growth defects in K562 and HCT116 cells.
source: DNMT1i treatment led to minimal growth defects in both cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Growth assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A demonstrates cell viability across DNMT1i doses.

claim: DNMT1i treatment increased CTCF binding at thousands of sites in K562 and HCT116 cells.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Maurano et al., 2015), DNMT1i treatment increased CTCF binding at thousands of sites, which we term 'DNMT1i-specific peaks' (2079 up- and 2 downregulated peaks in K562, 6686 up- and 328 downregulated peaks in HCT116).
evidence: ChIP-seq data showing differential CTCF binding between DNMT1i and DMSO conditions, with citation to prior work.

claim: DNMT1i-specific CTCF sites were 80-90% methylated in wild-type cells.
source: As expected, DNMT1i-specific CTCF sites were 80–90% methylated in wild-type cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Bisulfite sequencing data showing methylation levels at DNMT1i-specific peaks in wild-type cells.

claim: Half of the CTCF binding motifs enriched within DNMT1i-specific peak regions were methylated at two key CpG sites implicated in CTCF binding.
source: half of the CTCF binding motifs enriched within these peak regions were methylated at two key CpG sites implicated in CTCF binding (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Wang et al., 2012; Spracklin et al., 2023).
evidence: Motif methylation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C with citations to prior studies identifying key CpG sites.

claim: DNMT1i-specific CTCF sites at baseline are more methylated than constitutive CTCF sites.
source: Analysis of genome-wide bisulfite information obtained from LIMe-Hi-C in K562 treated with DMSO and DNMT1i (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) revealed that these DNMT1i-specific CTCF sites at baseline are more methylated than their constitutive counterparts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: LIMe-Hi-C bisulfite data comparing methylation levels between DNMT1i-specific and constitutive CTCF sites.

claim: Upon DNMT1i treatment for 3 days, methylation levels at DNMT1i-specific CTCF sites are reduced twofold.
source: Strikingly, upon treatment with the DNMT1i treatment for 3 days, methylation levels at DNMT1i-specific CTCF sites are reduced twofold (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: LIMe-Hi-C bisulfite data showing change in methylation at DNMT1i-specific sites after treatment.

claim: 45% of DNMT1i-specific peaks in K562 and 30% in HCT116 reside within at least one loop anchor.
source: CTCF HiChIP revealed that a large subset of DNMT1i-specific peaks (45% K562, 30% HCT116) resides within at least one loop anchor and these are henceforth called 'looping' peaks (see Methods) (Lareau and Aryee, 2018a; Lareau and Aryee, 2018b).
evidence: HiChIP data analysis quantifying the proportion of DNMT1i-specific peaks that participate in chromatin loops.

claim: Loops anchored by DNMT1i-specific peaks increase moderately in strength upon DNMT1 inhibition with an average log2fold-change of approximately 0.3.
source: On average, loops that are anchored by DNMT1i-specific peaks increase moderately in strength upon DNMT1 inhibition (average log2fold-change~0.3) (Figure 1E).
evidence: HiChIP loop strength analysis comparing DNMT1i to DMSO conditions.

claim: Hi-C interaction signal at DNMT1i-specific peaks increases following 3 days of DNMT1 inhibition.
source: Consistent with our Hi-ChIP data, this analysis revealed an increase in Hi-C interaction signal at DNMT1i-specific peaks following 3 days of DNMT1 inhibition (Figure 1F).
evidence: Aggregate pileup analysis of published LIMe-Hi-C data showing increased interaction frequency at DNMT1i-specific peaks.

claim: Loss of DNA methylation through DNMT1i treatment led to the preferential reactivation of CTCF peaks on non-intron gene bodies.
source: Consistent with previous findings using azacitidine (Maurano et al., 2015), loss of DNA methylation through DNMT1i treatment led to the preferential reactivation of CTCF peaks on non-intron gene bodies, with half of K562 DNMT1i-specific peaks emerging in exons, promoters, or transcription termination sites (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Genomic annotation analysis of DNMT1i-specific peaks with citation to prior work.

claim: Enrichment on gene bodies was particularly pronounced with looping DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks.
source: Notably, this enrichment on gene bodies was particularly pronounced with looping DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G, and H)
evidence: Comparison of genomic annotations between looping and non-looping DNMT1i-specific peaks.

claim: CTCF partners of DNMT1i-specific peaks tend to engage in a moderately greater total number of different loops compared to all CTCF peaks.
source: Notably, the CTCF partners of DNMT1i-specific peaks tend to engage in a moderately greater total number of different loops compared to all CTCF peaks (i.e. have more looping partners, Figure 2A), mostly for K562 cells (average increase ~1.3-fold).
evidence: HiChIP analysis quantifying the number of looping partners for CTCF peaks that interact with DNMT1i-specific peaks.

claim: Non-intronic gene body CTCF peaks more frequently participate in loops with highly looping CTCF partners compared to intronic or intergenic CTCF peaks.
source: This trend is in part driven by the tendency of non-intronic gene body CTCF peaks to more frequently participate in loops with highly looping CTCF partners in comparison to intronic or intergenic CTCF peaks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Analysis of looping partner characteristics stratified by genomic annotation of CTCF peaks.

claim: HiChIP loops between DNMT1i-specific peaks and highly looping peaks increased in strength upon DNMT1 inhibition with an average log2fold-change of approximately 0.3.
source: HiChIP loops between DNMT1i-specific peaks and highly looping peaks also increased in strength upon DNMT1 inhibition (average log2fold-change~0.3), consistent with increased interactions between these sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: HiChIP loop strength analysis for loops connecting DNMT1i-specific peaks to highly looping partners.

claim: Regions near highly looping CTCF peaks are accessible and modestly enriched for active chromatin marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac.
source: Similarly, regions near highly looping CTCF peaks are accessible and modestly enriched for active chromatin marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac (Figure 2D).
evidence: Aggregate profile analysis of public histone modification and ATAC-seq data over highly looping CTCF peaks.

claim: Highly looping CTCF sites have an approximately twofold stronger propensity to engage in chromatin interactions compared to ordinary CTCF sites based on Hi-C data.
source: Furthermore, based on previously published Hi-C data (Siegenfeld et al., 2022), highly looping CTCF sites have an approximately twofold stronger propensity to engage in chromatin interactions compared to ordinary CTCF sites (Figure 2E).
evidence: Aggregate pileup analysis of published Hi-C data centered on highly looping versus normal CTCF peaks.

claim: Stripe anchors identified from Hi-C data reside closer to highly looping CTCF peaks than all peaks.
source: In addition, stripe anchors identified from these Hi-C data also reside closer to highly looping CTCF peaks than all peaks, consistent with the similarities between these features (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Distance analysis between stripe anchors and highly looping versus all CTCF peaks.

claim: DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks and highly looping CTCF peaks are enriched in the A1 subcompartment of the genome.
source: In particular, we found an enrichment of DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks and highly looping CTCF peaks in the A1 subcompartment of the genome, which is differentiated from the A2 subcompartment largely due to its localization near nuclear speckles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Xiong and Ma, 2019).
evidence: Subcompartment annotation analysis of CTCF peak categories with citation to prior work defining A1 subcompartment characteristics.

claim: DNMT1i-specific peaks are located in regions of twofold higher SON signal compared to all CTCF peaks.
source: Consistent with their localization near speckles, DNMT1i-specific peaks are located in regions of twofold higher SON signal compared to all CTCF peaks (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: SON Cut&Tag signal quantification over DNMT1i-specific versus all CTCF peaks.

claim: The enrichment of DNMT1i-specific peaks near speckles is strongest for looping DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks.
source: Notably, this trend is strongest for looping DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks (Figure 2G).
evidence: SON Cut&Tag signal comparison between looping and non-looping DNMT1i-specific peaks.

claim: Enrichment of looping DNMT1i-specific peaks near speckles is corroborated by publicly available SON TSA-seq data in wild-type cells.
source: This enrichment of looping DNMT1i-specific peaks near speckles is further corroborated by publicly available SON TSA-seq data in wild-type cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: Analysis of public SON TSA-seq data over DNMT1i-specific peaks with citation to data source.

claim: Highly looping CTCF peaks are enriched at nuclear speckles with approximately 5-fold enrichment relative to all CTCF peaks.
source: Strikingly, relative to all CTCF peaks, highly looping CTCF peaks are enriched at nuclear speckles (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, ~5-fold enrichment).
evidence: SON Cut&Tag and TSA-seq signal quantification over highly looping versus all CTCF peaks.

claim: The number of different loops a CTCF peak engages in and their corresponding strength are positively correlated with SON Cut&Tag signal with Pearson R = 0.2.
source: More broadly, the number of different loops a CTCF peak engages in and their corresponding strength are positively correlated (Pearson R = 0.2) with SON Cut&Tag signal (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Correlation analysis between SON Cut&Tag signal and loop characteristics of CTCF peaks.

claim: CTCF peaks with strong Cut&Tag SON signal preferentially engage in strong shorter-range interactions in published Hi-C data.
source: In addition, we observed that CTCF peaks with strong Cut&Tag SON signal preferentially engage in strong shorter-range interactions in published Hi-C interaction data (Figure 2J; Siegenfeld et al., 2022).
evidence: Aggregate pileup analysis of published Hi-C data stratified by SON signal at CTCF peaks.

claim: DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks gain approximately 3-fold SON Cut&Tag signal upon DNMT1i treatment.
source: We found that DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks gain ~3-fold SON Cut&Tag signal upon DNMT1i treatment (Figure 3C).
evidence: SON Cut&Tag signal comparison at DNMT1i-specific peaks between DNMT1i and DMSO conditions.

claim: The gain in SON signal at DNMT1i-specific peaks is blocked when CTCF is degraded by HaloPROTAC3 treatment.
source: This gain in SON signal is blocked when CTCF is degraded by HaloPROTAC3 treatment, suggesting that speckle association at these DNMT1i-specific sites is dependent on CTCF (Figure 3C).
evidence: SON Cut&Tag signal at DNMT1i-specific peaks in DNMT1i treatment with and without CTCF degradation.

claim: Acute CTCF degradation altered the expression of hundreds of genes, with approximately equal numbers up- and downregulated (488 upregulated, 338 downregulated).
source: Consistent with prior studies (Nora et al., 2017), acute CTCF degradation altered the expression of hundreds of genes, with approximately equal numbers up- and downregulated (488 upregulated, 338 downregulated, p-adj<0.05, |log2fold-change|>0.5) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: RNA-seq differential expression analysis following CTCF degradation with citation to prior work.

claim: DNMT1i treatment for 24 hours primarily resulted in gene upregulation, with 135 genes upregulated and 8 genes downregulated.
source: As expected, DNMT1i treatment in this cell line for 24 hr primarily resulted in gene upregulation, with 135 genes upregulated and 8 genes downregulated (p-adj<0.05, |log2fold-change|>0.5) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: RNA-seq differential expression analysis following DNMT1i treatment.

claim: Genes in Cluster 2 preferentially gained CTCF occupancy upon DNMT1 inhibition compared to genes in other clusters.
source: Notably, genes in Cluster 2 preferentially gained CTCF occupancy upon DNMT1 inhibition compared to genes in other clusters (Figure 3D, right, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: CTCF ChIP-seq analysis showing change in CTCF binding at genes in different expression clusters.

claim: Genes in Cluster 2 have nearly threefold higher SON TSA-seq levels than genes in Cluster 4.
source: Intriguingly, genes in Cluster 2 have nearly threefold higher SON TSA-seq levels than genes in Cluster 4 (Figure 3E)
evidence: SON TSA-seq signal quantification over genes in different expression clusters.

claim: Genes in Cluster 2 gain a modest level of SON Cut&Tag signal (log2fold-change approximately 0.1) upon DNMT1i treatment.
source: Moreover, genes in Cluster 2 gain a modest (log2fold-change~0.1) level of SON Cut&Tag signal upon DNMT1i treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: SON Cut&Tag signal change analysis at genes in Cluster 2 upon DNMT1i treatment.

claim: Treatment of the K562 FKBP12F36V double knock-in cell line with dTAG-13 resulted in near-complete degradation of both SON and SRRM2 within 6 hours.
source: Treatment of the K562 FKBP12F36V double knock-in cell line with dTAG-13 resulted in near-complete degradation of both SON and SRRM2 within 6 hr (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and western blot data showing depletion of SON and SRRM2 proteins after dTAG-13 treatment.

claim: Upon speckle degradation, 541 genes were downregulated and 184 genes were upregulated.
source: Upon speckle degradation, 541 genes were downregulated and 184 genes were upregulated (p-adj<0.05, |log2fold-change|>0.25) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: RNA-seq differential expression analysis following speckle degradation.

claim: Over 80% of downregulated genes upon speckle degradation were located within the closest decile to nuclear speckles by TSA-seq.
source: Consistent with a role of nuclear speckles in promoting transcription, over 80% of downregulated genes were located within the closest decile to nuclear speckles by TSA-seq (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Analysis of TSA-seq signal at genes downregulated upon speckle degradation.

claim: Genes with the highest SON Cut&Tag signal exhibited the strongest decrease in RNA abundance upon speckle degradation.
source: genes with the highest SON Cut&Tag signal exhibited the strongest decrease in RNA abundance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Correlation analysis between SON Cut&Tag signal and gene expression change upon speckle degradation.

claim: CTCF occupancy remained unchanged upon speckle degradation, with only two significantly downregulated peaks.
source: In contrast to the immediate RNA effects, CTCF occupancy remained unchanged upon speckle degradation, with only two significantly downregulated peaks (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: CTCF ChIP-seq comparison between speckle degradation and control conditions.

claim: CTCF HiChIP revealed that loop strength was largely unchanged across speckle Cut&Tag and TSA-seq quantiles upon speckle degradation.
source: CTCF HiChIP also revealed that loop strength was largely unchanged across speckle Cut&Tag and TSA-seq quantiles (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: HiChIP loop strength analysis stratified by speckle association after speckle degradation.

claim: After 12 hours of dTAG treatment, there was only a very subtle decrease in CTCF looping near speckles.
source: Even after 12 hr of dTAG treatment, there was only a very subtle decrease in CTCF looping near speckles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: HiChIP loop strength analysis at 12 hour timepoint of speckle degradation.

claim: Changes in gene expression upon speckle degradation were not associated with changes in loop strength or CTCF binding.
source: In addition, changes in gene expression were not associated with changes in loop strength or CTCF binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: Integrated analysis of gene expression changes, CTCF binding, and loop strength upon speckle degradation.

claim: Depleting CTCF for 24 hours did not noticeably change speckle morphology.
source: Conversely, depleting CTCF for 24 hr in our HaloTag-CTCF HCT116 knock-in cell line did not noticeably change speckle morphology (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging of speckle proteins SON and SRRM2 after CTCF degradation.

claim: DNA methylation hinders CTCF binding.
source: While it is established that DNA methylation hinders CTCF binding, the impacts of this methylation-sensitive CTCF binding on chromatin architecture and transcription are poorly defined.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: The insulator protein CTCF is essential for mediating chromatin loops and regulating gene expression.
source: The insulator protein CTCF is essential for mediating chromatin loops and regulating gene expression.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about CTCF function.

claim: CTCF establishes the anchors of many DNA loops and TADs likely by blocking loop extrusion by cohesin.
source: The architectural protein CTCF establishes the anchors of many DNA loops and TADs likely by blocking loop extrusion by cohesin (Nora et al., 2017; Wendt et al., 2008; Li et al., 2020; Fudenberg et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2019; Davidson et al., 2019; Xiang and Corces, 2021; Hansen et al., 2018; Sanborn et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Perturbation of CTCF binding sites at domain boundaries can lead to aberrant cross-domain enhancer-promoter contacts linked to gene misexpression in cancer and developmental disorders.
source: Consequently, perturbation of CTCF binding sites at domain boundaries can lead to aberrant cross-domain enhancer-promoter contacts, which have been linked to gene misexpression in cancer and developmental disorders (Dubois et al., 2022; Spielmann et al., 2018; Lupiáñez et al., 2015; Flavahan et al., 2016; Flavahan et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: CTCF binding and looping on or near genes can directly enforce enhancer-promoter loops and facilitate differential splicing and polyadenylation.
source: Furthermore, CTCF binding and looping on or near genes can directly enforce enhancer-promoter loops and facilitate differential splicing and polyadenylation (Rinzema et al., 2022; Kubo et al., 2021; Shukla et al., 2011; Ruiz-Velasco et al., 2017; Nanavaty et al., 2020; Alharbi et al., 2021; López Soto and Lipscombe, 2020; van Steensel and Furlong, 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Acute depletion of CTCF only leads to moderate transcriptional defects.
source: Although these examples demonstrate that CTCF can modulate transcription in specific contexts, acute depletion of CTCF only leads to moderate transcriptional defects, highlighting the complex and nuanced roles of CTCF in regulating gene expression (Rao et al., 2017; Nora et al., 2017; Schoenfelder and Fraser, 2019; Vermunt et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Global DNA demethylation causes the emergence of hundreds to thousands of previously masked CTCF peaks.
source: CTCF binding is sensitive to DNA methylation (Monteagudo-Sánchez et al., 2024a), and consequently, global DNA demethylation causes the emergence of hundreds to thousands of previously masked CTCF peaks (Bell and Felsenfeld, 2000; Hark et al., 2000; Hashimoto et al., 2017; Maurano et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Methylation-sensitive CTCF sites comprise only a small subset of all potential methylated CTCF sites.
source: However, these methylation-sensitive sites comprise only a small subset of all potential methylated CTCF sites, suggesting that DNA methylation serves as a specialized mechanism to regulate specific CTCF binding sites (Maurano et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement with citation to prior work and inference about mechanism.

claim: DNA methylation regulates a subset of CTCF loops and CTCF-dependent genes during mESC differentiation.
source: Moreover, recent work has revealed that DNA methylation regulates a subset of CTCF loops and CTCF-dependent genes during mESC differentiation (Monteagudo-Sánchez et al., 2024b).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Nuclear speckles are condensate bodies of protein and RNA that have been implicated in transcription and splicing.
source: Remarkably, DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks and their highly looping partners are located close to nuclear speckles – condensate bodies of protein and RNA that have been implicated in transcription and splicing (Chen et al., 2018; Chen and Belmont, 2019; Zhang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Spector and Lamond, 2011; Alexander et al., 2021; Ilık and Aktaş, 2022).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Subnuclear localization relative to nuclear landmarks such as nuclear speckles is linked to genome structure and function.
source: Subnuclear localization relative to nuclear landmarks such as nuclear speckles is linked to genome structure and function
evidence: Statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: Selective, noncovalent DNMT1 inhibitors enable dynamic control of DNA methylation with fewer undesirable effects such as DNA damage and cytotoxicity compared to earlier hypomethylating agents.
source: Recently, selective, noncovalent DNMT1 inhibitors (e.g. GSK3484862) have become available, enabling dynamic control of DNA methylation with fewer undesirable effects such as DNA damage and cytotoxicity (Azevedo Portilho et al., 2021; Pappalardi et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement about properties of DNMT1 inhibitors supported by citations.

claim: DNMT1i-specific peaks overlap with CTCF peaks in other cell types.
source: These peaks are known to overlap with CTCF peaks in other cell types (Maurano et al., 2015; Spracklin et al., 2023; Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Architectural stripes may contribute to transcription by promoting enhancer contacts with gene bodies.
source: Architectural stripes may contribute to transcription by promoting enhancer contacts with gene bodies (Vian et al., 2018; Yoon et al., 2022; Barrington et al., 2019; Kraft et al., 2019)
evidence: Statement about potential mechanism supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Architectural stripes may represent a mechanism to poise transcription.
source: and may also represent a mechanism to poise transcription (Barrington et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculative statement about mechanism supported by citation.

claim: Subcompartments near nuclear speckles exhibit increased CTCF binding and looping.
source: Strikingly, DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks and their highly looping partners are located near nuclear speckles, consistent with prior studies, showing that subcompartments near nuclear speckles exhibit increased CTCF binding and looping (Wang et al., 2021; Jabbari et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Nuclear speckles are hubs of DNA-DNA contacts.
source: Studies have shown that nuclear speckles are hubs of DNA-DNA contacts (Spector and Lamond, 2011; Ilık and Aktaş, 2022; Brown et al., 2008; Ilik et al., 2020; Faber et al., 2022; Quinodoz et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: CTCF can form stress-responsive clusters near nuclear speckles in some cell types.
source: Additionally, CTCF can form stress-responsive clusters near nuclear speckles in some cell types, and genomic subcompartments associated with speckles have been correlated with increased CTCF binding and looping (Chen et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021; Jabbari et al., 2019; Lehman et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: A direct connection between nuclear speckles and CTCF binding and looping has not been extensively explored.
source: However, a direct connection between nuclear speckles and CTCF binding and looping has not been extensively explored.
evidence: Statement about gap in knowledge in the field.

claim: Previous work knocking down SRRM2 supports a causative role of speckles in modulating chromatin structure but did not specifically study changes in CTCF binding or looping.
source: Previous work knocking down SRRM2 supports a causative role of speckles in modulating chromatin structure but did not specifically study changes in CTCF binding or looping (Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about prior work with citation.

claim: CTCF clustering and looping is not dependent on phase separation or nuclear bodies.
source: This notion is consistent with recent work, showing that CTCF clustering and looping is not dependent on phase separation or nuclear bodies (Lee et al., 2022; Ulianov et al., 2021)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Transcriptional disruption does not immediately impact chromatin looping or CTCF binding.
source: and that transcriptional disruption does not immediately impact chromatin looping or CTCF binding (Vian et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2020; Luan et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: DNA methylation may modulate genome architecture by protecting a subset of genic CTCF sites from engaging with promiscuous CTCF peaks located near nuclear speckles.
source: Taken altogether, our findings highlight one possible mechanism through which DNA methylation may modulate genome architecture – by protecting a subset of genic CTCF sites from engaging with promiscuous CTCF peaks located near nuclear speckles.
evidence: Proposed model based on integration of experimental findings.

claim: Genes near nuclear speckles may be particularly susceptible to activation through CTCF-dependent mechanisms.
source: Genes near nuclear speckles may be particularly susceptible to activation through CTCF-dependent mechanisms, and thus might require this layer of protective regulation.
evidence: Speculative statement about mechanism based on findings.

claim: The GC-rich composition of non-intron gene bodies might increase the likelihood of CTCF motifs in comparison to other genomic regions.
source: Furthermore, the GC-rich composition of non-intron gene bodies might increase the likelihood of CTCF motifs in comparison to other genomic regions, increasing the vulnerability of these sites to ectopic CTCF binding.
evidence: Speculative statement about sequence composition and CTCF binding.

claim: DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks preferentially form chromatin loops on gene bodies.
source: We found that DNMT1i-specific peaks preferentially form chromatin loops on gene bodies and interact with highly looping partner peaks located in regions of active chromatin.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from HiChIP and genomic annotation analyses.

claim: DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks interact with highly looping partner peaks located in regions of active chromatin.
source: We found that DNMT1i-specific peaks preferentially form chromatin loops on gene bodies and interact with highly looping partner peaks located in regions of active chromatin.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from HiChIP and chromatin state analyses.

claim: Both DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks and their highly looping partners are enriched near nuclear speckles.
source: Notably, both DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks and their highly looping partners are enriched near nuclear speckles – condensate bodies implicated in transcription and splicing.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from SON Cut&Tag and TSA-seq analyses.

claim: CTCF is important for DNMT1i-dependent interactions between chromatin and speckle proteins.
source: By degrading CTCF upon DNMT1 inhibition, we revealed that CTCF is important for DNMT1i-dependent interactions between chromatin and speckle proteins.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from CTCF degradation and SON Cut&Tag experiments.

claim: CTCF promotes the activation of genes near speckles upon DNMT1 inhibition.
source: Moreover, we found that CTCF promotes the activation of genes near speckles upon DNMT1 inhibition.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from CTCF degradation and RNA-seq experiments.

claim: Nuclear speckles influence RNA abundance but do not maintain CTCF binding or looping.
source: Conversely, acute depletion of nuclear speckles revealed that they influence RNA abundance but do not maintain CTCF binding or looping.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from speckle degradation experiments with RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and HiChIP.

claim: DNA methylation prevents spurious CTCF occupancy and interactions with regulatory elements near nuclear speckles.
source: Collectively, our study suggests a model wherein DNA methylation prevents spurious CTCF occupancy and interactions with regulatory elements near nuclear speckles, yet CTCF looping is robust toward the loss of speckles.
evidence: Proposed model integrating findings from DNMT1i, CTCF degradation, and speckle degradation experiments.

claim: CTCF looping is robust toward the loss of speckles.
source: Collectively, our study suggests a model wherein DNA methylation prevents spurious CTCF occupancy and interactions with regulatory elements near nuclear speckles, yet CTCF looping is robust toward the loss of speckles.
evidence: Proposed model based on findings from speckle degradation experiments showing minimal impact on CTCF looping.

claim: DNMT1i-specific peaks enable transcriptional activation by interacting with regulatory elements through highly looping CTCF partner peaks.
source: Thus, we propose that DNMT1i-specific peaks enable transcriptional activation by interacting with regulatory elements through highly looping CTCF partner peaks (Figure 4E).
evidence: Proposed model based on integration of looping, chromatin state, and gene expression findings.

claim: DNA demethylation causes pleiotropic effects ranging from changes in gene expression to transcription factor binding.
source: However, DNA demethylation causes pleiotropic effects ranging from changes in gene expression to transcription factor binding (Azevedo Portilho et al., 2021; Yin et al., 2017), and we cannot rule out that these other features could contribute to the effects we observe.
evidence: Statement about limitations with citations to prior work.

claim: A role of CTCF in facilitating chromatin loops near speckles is synergistic with proposed models suggesting that intragenic looping contributes to gene splicing.
source: A role of CTCF in facilitating chromatin loops near speckles is synergistic with proposed models, suggesting that intragenic looping contributes to gene splicing (Ruiz-Velasco et al., 2017; Liao and Regev, 2021).
evidence: Statement connecting findings to prior models with citations.

claim: DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks may reorganize genes near nuclear speckles as a means of influencing transcription.
source: Thus, DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks may reorganize genes near nuclear speckles as a means of influencing transcription.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on integration of findings.

claim: The genome interactions disrupted upon SRRM2 depletion are not mediated by CTCF or only occur after a longer time.
source: Our findings also suggest that the genome interactions disrupted upon SRRM2 depletion (Hu et al., 2019) are not mediated by CTCF or only occur after a longer time.
evidence: Inference based on findings from speckle degradation experiments with citation to prior work.

claim: Nuclear speckles may contribute to the establishment, but not maintenance, of CTCF loops.
source: However, it is possible that nuclear speckles contribute to the establishment, but not maintenance, of CTCF loops, which may not be evident in our system due to the short time points employed for speckle degradation.
evidence: Speculative statement about alternative interpretation of findings.

claim: Other features enriched near speckles, such as open chromatin, high GC content, and active gene expression, could contribute to increased CTCF binding and looping near speckles.
source: Moreover, other features enriched near speckles, such as open chromatin, high GC content, and active gene expression, could instead contribute to increased CTCF binding and looping near speckles.
evidence: Speculative statement about alternative explanations for observed correlations.

claim: This study achieved the first acute degradation of nuclear speckles.
source: We next studied whether speckles impact CTCF binding or looping by achieving the first acute degradation of nuclear speckles.
evidence: Statement about novelty of experimental approach.

claim: Long-term SON depletion causes mitotic arrest.
source: To accomplish this, we sought to acutely degrade speckles to evaluate whether speckles actively maintain CTCF loops while mitigating confounding factors associated with mitotic arrest caused by long-term SON depletion (Ahn et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement about known effect of long-term SON depletion with citation.

claim: A subset of genes enriched for methylation-sensitive CTCF binding depends on CTCF for expression upon DNMT1i treatment.
source: Thus, these data demonstrate that a subset of genes enriched for methylation-sensitive CTCF binding depends on CTCF for expression upon DNMT1i treatment.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from integrated CTCF degradation, RNA-seq, and ChIP-seq analyses.

claim: SON associates with DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks in a CTCF-dependent manner.
source: Thus, SON associates with DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks in a CTCF-dependent manner.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from CTCF degradation and SON Cut&Tag experiments.

claim: CTCF is necessary for both gene activation and speckle protein association upon DNMT1 inhibition.
source: Taken together, these experiments show that CTCF is necessary for both gene activation and speckle protein association upon DNMT1 inhibition.
evidence: Summary statement integrating findings from CTCF degradation experiments with RNA-seq and SON Cut&Tag.

claim: Upon DNA demethylation, DNMT1i-specific CTCF sites form loops to highly looping partners associated with active regulatory marks and stripe anchors.
source: Thus, these results show that upon DNA demethylation, DNMT1i-specific CTCF sites form loops to highly looping partners associated with active regulatory marks and stripe anchors.
evidence: Summary statement integrating findings from HiChIP, chromatin state analysis, and stripe analysis.

claim: Acute disruption of speckles supports their direct involvement in RNA abundance.
source: Although acute disruption of speckles supports their direct involvement in RNA abundance, we observed minimal impacts on CTCF binding or looping.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from speckle degradation experiments with RNA-seq.

claim: Speckle degradation clarifies the directionality of the relationship between speckles and CTCF.
source: Overall, our speckle degradation experiments help clarify the directionality of the relationship between speckles and CTCF.
evidence: Summary statement about the contribution of speckle degradation experiments to understanding causality.

claim: Selective DNMT1 inhibition leads to the emergence of thousands of DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks on gene bodies that engage in new chromatin interactions.
source: Altogether, selective DNMT1 inhibition leads to the emergence of thousands of DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks on gene bodies that engage in new chromatin interactions.
evidence: Summary statement integrating findings from ChIP-seq and HiChIP experiments.

claim: DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks interact with highly looping partners located near nuclear speckles.
source: Overall, our results reveal that DNMT1i-specific CTCF peaks interact with highly looping partners located near nuclear speckles.
evidence: Summary statement integrating findings from HiChIP and SON Cut&Tag/TSA-seq analyses.
